parties:
Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, Zonal Office, Rajshahi ------ Plaintiff-Appellant
vs.
Rowshan Ara Begum --------- Defendant-Respondent
full_judgment:
Md. Bashir Ullah, J : At the instance of the plaintiff in Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 2013, this appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 17-6-2019 passed by the learned District Judge, Rajshahi in the aforesaid case dismissing the same. 

2. The salient facts leading to preferring this appeal are: 
Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation, Zonal Office, Rajshahi (briefly "the Corporation") as plaintiff filed the said Miscellaneous case for realisation of Taka 11,22,682.77 from the defendant contending inter alia that, the defendant applied to the plaintiff, Corporation for a loan to construct a house in the scheduled land. Then the plaintiff sanctioned Taka 4,10,000 in favour of the defendant with interest at the rate of 10% per annum on 9-2-1983 under sanction letter No. Raj/118. Subsequently, the plaintiff sanctioned another loan amounting to Taka 47,000. The said loan was scheduled to be repaid within 30 years with monthly installment at Taka 3,548.45. However, the defendant failed to repay the loan amount as per condition of the sanction letter and thus, the default loan amount with interest stood at Taka 9,93,093.84 and that of another at Taka 1,29,588.93 totaling at Taka 11,22,682.77 and hence the plaintiff prayed for a decree for the realisation of the said amount with interest. 

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written objection denying all material averments so made in the plaint. It has been stated that there is no cause of action to file the suit. The case has been filed suppressing the facts as earlier, the plaintiff filed Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1992 before the Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Rajshahi for realisation of Taka 8,08,897.23 and the Miscellaneous Case was allowed on 3-10-1993. The defendant adjusted entire liability by paying Taka 9,14,400. After repayment, the defendant requested the plaintiff to return the mortgage deed and other documents as there is no liability. However, the plaintiff did not return the deed and documents. 

4. When the defendant sent a legal notice to the plaintiff, Corporation through her lawyer on 6-4-2015 and as the plaintiff did not return the documents the defendant then filed Other Class Suit No. 122 of 2016 before the Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar Court, Rajshahi for getting the deed and documents lying with the plaintiff, Corporation. The plaintiff did not mention in its plaint about the Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1992 and Other Class Suit No. 122 of 2016. Hence, the defendant prayed for dismissing the suit. 

5. The trial Court framed as many as 04(four) different issues and in course of the trial, the plaintiff examined 01(one) witness and defendant examined 01 (one) witness and both parties adduced documentary evidence in order to prove their respective cases. 

6. Upon hearing, the parties and on perusal of the pleadings, the learned District Judge, Rajshahi dismissed the miscellaneous case on 17-6-2019. 

7. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 17-6-2019 passed by the District Judge, Rajshahi the plaintiff as appellant then preferred the instant appeal. 

8. Mr. Md. Zahirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant submits that, the learned District Judge, Rajshahi erred in law and fact in passing the impugned judgment and order and therefore the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. 

9. He next submits that, the learned District Judge did not provide any cogent findings on assessing the evidence on record and without considering the documentary evidence dismissed the miscellaneous case by the impugned judgment and order and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside. With such submission, the learned Advocate finally prays for allowing the instant Appeal. 

10. None represented on behalf of the opposite party. 

11. We have heard the learned Advocate for the appellant, perused the memorandum of appeal, impugned judgment and order passed by the trial Court and other materials on record.

12. We find from the deposition of OPW 1 Md. Mamun who stated in his chief that, the defendant adjusted the entire liability, complying with the judgment and decree passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1992 filed earlier even then the plaintiff filed the miscellaneous case against the defendant. The PW 1 Farzana Hossen, Principal Officer (Law) could not deny the claim of the defendant. PW 1, further stated in her cross-examination that, 
বিগত ৩-১০-১৯৯৩ খ্রিঃ তারিখে ৮৮/৯২ নং অর্থঋণ মোকদ্দমার রায় ও ডিক্রি হইতে পারে। গত ৬-১১-৯৩ খ্রিঃ তারিখে ১ম কিস্তির টাকা দেওয়া হইতে পারে। ঐ মোকদ্দমায় তাহাদের দাবী ৮,০৮,৮৯৭.২৩ টাকা ছিল কিনা বলিতে পারবেন না। প্রতিপক্ষ ৯,১৪,৪০০ টাকা পরিশোধ করিয়াছেন কিনা জানেন না। ঋণের টাকা পরিশোধ সাপেক্ষে বন্ধকী কাগজপত্র ফেরত দেওয়ার কথা ছিল কিনা বলতে পারবেন না। কাগজপত্র ফেরতের জন্য ৬-৪-১৫ খ্রিঃ তারিখে তাদেরকে লিগ্যাল নোটিশ দেওয়া হয় কিনা জানেন না। লিগ্যাল নোটিশ দেওয়া সত্বেও কাগজপত্র ফেরত না দেওয়ায় সদর সিনিয়র সহকারী জজ আদালতে অঃ প্রঃ ১২২/১৬ নং মোকদ্দমা এই মামলার প্রতিপক্ষ দাখিল করে কিনা জানেন না। এই মোকদ্দমায় হাউজ বিল্ডিং ফাইনান্স কর্পোরেশন জবাব দাখিল করে কিনা জানেন না।

13. Since the plaintiff earlier filed Miscellaneous Case No. 88 of 1992 before the then Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Rajshahi, it cannot file Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 2013 before the District Judge, Rajshahi on similar issue. 

14. The District Judge, Rajshahi very rightly observed that-
অর্থঋণ আদালতের ৮৮/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমার রায় ও ডিক্রিতে অসন্তুষ্ট হইয়া থাকিলে দরখাস্তকারী উক্ত রায় ও ডিক্রির বিরুদ্ধে আইনানুগ পদক্ষেপ গ্রহণ করিতে পারিতেন। কিন্তু তাহা করেন নাই। উক্ত মোকদ্দমার রায় ডিক্রিতে আদালতের পর্যবেক্ষনে কোন ভুল থাকিলে তাহার বিরুদ্ধে উচ্চ আদালতে প্রতিকার প্রার্থনার সুযোগ ছিল। কিন্তু হাউজ বিল্ডিং ফাইন্যান্স কর্পোরেশন তাহাও করেন নাই। .. হাউজ বিল্ডিং ফাইন্যান্স কর্পোরেশন তাহাদের বার্থ্যতার দায়ভার গোপন করিয়া অত্র মিস কেস আনয়ন করিয়াছে, যাহা অনাকাঙ্খিত ও অনভিপ্রেত।
 
15. It appears that, the case was filed by suppressing the facts so the subsequent Miscellaneous Case is barred by the principle of res-judicata and the case should not have been filed at all which is unfortunate and unwarranted as no one shall be vexed twice when the issue has been fairly and finally decided in a former suit. Once an issue has been finally decided it cannot be re-agitated by the same parties. 

16. Given the above facts and circumstances, we do not find any illegality or impropriety in the impugned judgment and order, which calls for no interference by this Court. Therefore, we do not find any substance in the appeal. 

17. Resultantly, the appeal is dismissed, however without any order as to cost. 

18. The judgment and order dated 17-6-2019 passed by the learned District Judge, Rajshahi in Miscellaneous Case No. 40 of 2013 is thus sustained and affirmed. 

Let a copy of the judgment along with the lower Court's record be transmitted to the concerned Court forthwith. 

End.

lawyer:
Lutfor Rahman, Advocate—For the Appellant. 
M.M. Shafifullah, Advocate—For the Respondent Nos. 1-4.
parties:
Firoza Begum ------ Plaintiff-Appellant
vs
Limo Electronics Limited and others ------- Defendants-Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Bashir Ullah, J: At the instance of the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 51 of 2019, this appeal is directed against the judgment and decree dated 21-8-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in the aforesaid Title Suit rejecting the plaint against the defendant Nos. 1-4 on contest. 

2. The precise facts leading to preferring this appeal are:—
The present appellant as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit before the Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka on 23-1-2019 seeking the following reliefs:— 
“ক) বিবাদীগণ তফসিল বর্ণিত ফ্ল্যাটটি বাদী বরাবরে রেজিস্ট্রি করিয়া দিতে বাধ্য মর্মে এক ঘোষণামূলক ডিক্রী প্রদান করিতে;
খ) বাদীপক্ষে চুক্তি অনুযায়ী তফসিল বর্ণিত ফ্ল্যাটটি বাদীর বরাবরে রেজিষ্ট্রি করিয়া দেওয়ার এক নির্দেশনামূলক ডিক্রী প্রদান করিতে;
গ) বিবাদীপক্ষ ফ্ল্যাটটি রেজিস্ট্রি না দিলে আদালতযোগে রেজিষ্ট্রির নির্দেশ প্রদানের এক ডিক্রী প্রদান করিতে;
ঘ) বিজ্ঞ ৫ম যুগ্ম জেলা জজ আদালতে বিচারাধীন ২/২০১৯ নং মানী মোকদ্দমা নিষ্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত তফসিল বর্ণিত সম্পত্তিতে বাদীর নিরঙ্কুশ ও শান্তিপূর্ণ দখল হইতে অবৈধভাবে উচ্ছেদ না করিতে পারে মর্মে এক ডিক্রী প্রদান করিতে;
ঙ) নালিশের সম্যক ব্যয় বাদীর অনুকূলে এবং বিবাদীর প্রতিকূলে ডিক্রি দিতে;
চ) আদালতের ন্যায় বিচারে বাদী আর যে সকল বৈধ প্রতিকার পাইবার হকদার উহার সম্যক বাদীর অনুকূলে এবং বিবাদীর প্রতিকূলে ডিক্রি দিতে আজ্ঞা হয়।"

3. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the plaintiff was appointed on 6-5-2001 as the Personal Secretary to the Managing Director of the defendant No.1 company, wherein her husband was also employed as Project Manager. Defendant Nos. 2 and 3, being pleased and satisfied with their services, orally gifted the flat described in the schedule to the plaintiff. Since 1-11-2001, the plaintiff, along with her husband, has been residing there in the flat duly paying all utility charges. Subsequently, in March 2003, the defendants asked the plaintiff and her husband to purchase the flat, which had earlier been gifted to them. The purchase price of the flat was fixed at Taka 30,00,000 (thirty lac) only. Out of the said amount, Taka 5,00,000 (five lac) was adjusted by the defendants from the receivable commission of the plaintiff's husband, and the remaining sum of Taka 25,00,000 (twenty five lac) was agreed to be paid through deductions from the salary of the plaintiff in monthly installments of Taka 10,000 (ten thousand). However, from September 2014, the defendants abruptly ceased payment of the plaintiff's salary without assigning any reason. Thereafter, in November 2018, the defendants asked the plaintiff to resign from service and vacate the suit flat. Feeling aggrieved, the plaintiff filed Money Suit No.. 02 of 2019 against the defendants for recovery of arrears of salary amounting to Taka 10,51,500 (ten lac fifty one thousand and five hundred). Subsequently, on 21-1-2019, the defendants again threatened the plaintiff with eviction from the suit flat. Under such circumstances, the plaintiff instituted the suit. 

4. On 7-4-2019, the defendant nos. 1-4 entered appearance and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure stating that the plaint is liable to be rejected as the same is barred by law. The plaintiff filed a written objection against the said application stating that the application is not maintainable as the defendants did not file written statement. Subsequently, on 20-5-2019 the defendant No. 1-4 filed written statement denying the material allegations so made in the plaint and stated that the suit is not maintainable in its present form, the suit is barred by limitation and section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. 

5. The learned Judge of the trial Court upon hearing the parties and considering of materials on record rejected the plaint on contest by impugned judgment and decree dated 21-8-2019. 

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment and decree dated 21-8-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka the plaintiff as appellant preferred this appeal. 

7. Mr. Lutfor Rahman, the learned counsel appearing for the appellant upon taking us to the impugned judgment and decree at the very outset submits that the trial Court has erroneously rejected the plaint without considering the facts and circumstances of the case and law so placed before it. 

8. He further contends that the gift has already been acted upon and the trial Court failed to appreciate that the plaintiff can prove her case by adducing evidence at the time of trial and hence, the impugned judgment is liable to be set-aside. 

9. The learned counsel also contends that the appellant has been in exclusive, uninterrupted and peaceful possession in the suit property and paying electricity bills, WASA bills, Gas bills and other charges of the suit flat till date, but without considering the possession the trial Court rejected the plaint in a slipshod manner illegally and arbitrarily. 

10. In support of his contention, the learned counsel for the appellant has referred to the decisions passed in the cases of Saifiuddin Ahmed vs Dr. Hosne Ara Begum alias Golap and others, reported in XIII ADC (2016) 498 and Kari Moulavi Abdul Gafur and another vs Mohammad Nurullah alias Badsha, reported in 6 LM (AD) (2019)190. With these submissions and relying on the decisions the learned counsel finally prays for allowing the appeal by setting aside the impugned judgment and decree. 

11. Per contra, Mr. MM Shafiullah, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent nos. 1-4 vehemently opposes the contention taken by the learned counsel for the appellant and contends that there is no existence of any agreement regarding the alleged gift. 

12. He further contends that no oral gift is permissible under Hindu Law and for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property, the transfer must be in writing and effected by a registered instrument signed by the donor and attested by at least two witnesses under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act which is absent in the instant case. In support of his such contention, he referred to the decisions passed in the case of Kala Miah vs Copal Chandra Paul and others, reported in 51 DLR 77. 

13. He next contends that, the trial Court has very rightly rejected the plaint since the suit is a fruitless one as the ultimate result of the suit is as clear as day light and such type of suit should be buried in its inception. In support of his contention, he then relied upon the decision passed in the case of Abdul Jalil and others vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Limited and others, reported in 53 DLR (AD) 12. 

14. The learned counsel also contends that no gift was made to the plaintiff by the defendants nor was any contract or agreement executed between the plaintiff and the defendants concerning the suit flat and, as such„ no legal obligation or enforceable right within the meaning of section 55 of the Specific Relief Act has arisen in favour of the plaintiff and therefore, the plaintiff is not entitled to a decree of mandatory injunction as :)rayed for. In support of his contention, he referred to the decisions passed in the case of Aftabuddin vs Mahfiizus Sobhan and others, reported in 1990 BLD (AD) 47:42 DLR (AD) 78. 

15. With those submissions, the learned counsel finally prays for dismissing the appeal by affirming the impugned judgment and decree. 

16. We have considered the submission so advanced by the learned counsel for the appellant and that of the respondents at length, perused the memorandum of appeal, supplementary affidavit, application for injunction and the impugned judgment and decree. 

17. On going through the plaint, we find that the plaintiff who is a Muslim by religion claimed that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 belonging to Hindu community made an oral gift of the suit flat. The plaintiff sought for a declaration that the defendants are bound to register the suit flat in her favour. But it is settled proposition of law that under Hindu Law, oral gift is not valid and permissible in view of the provision of section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act. Under section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, for the purpose of making a gift of immovable property valid, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor and attested by at least two witnesses. An oral gift of immovable property by a Hindu, even followed by possession, does not create any legal rights in favour of the donee and is void in the eye of law. 

18. In Hari Kison Panday vs Nageswari Debi and others, reported in 8 DLR 65 it has been held that a gift under the Transfer of Property Act can only be effected in the manner provided by section 123. 

19. In Kalu Miah vs Gopal Chandra Paul and others, (supra) it has been held:— 
"In the absence of a registered instrument a gift by a person belonging to Hindu Community (governed by the Dayabhaga School of Hindu Law) is not valid under section 123 of the Act." 

20. The plaint shows the acquisition of plaintiff's title in the suit flat is based on an alleged oral gift made by defendant nos. 2 and 3 who belong to the Hindu religion is explicitly and expressly barred by law where a court is always reluctant to proceed with a suit which would be a futile exercise. 

21. In the plaint, the plaintiff claimed that the price of the suit flat was fixed at Taka 30,00,000 (thirty lac) and Taka 5,00,000 (five lac) was adjusted as of commission of the plaintiff's husband and rest Taka 25,00,000 (twenty five lac) was deducted from the salary of the plaintiff. In this regard, no documents were produced before the trial Court. The trial Court in its judgment observed that "নালিশী ফ্ল্যাটের মূল্য ৩০ লক্ষ টাকা নির্ধারণ করা হয় এবং যার মধ্যে ২৫ লক্ষ টাকা বাদীর বেতন থেকে সমন্বয় করা হইয়াছে এবং বাকী ৫ লক্ষ টাকা বাদীর স্বামীর কমিশন থেকে প্রদান করা হইয়াছে। কিন্তু এইরূপ কোন বায়নাপত্র অথবা চুক্তিপত্র বা অন্য কোন দালিলিক কাগজপত্র আদালতে দাখিল করা হয় না।" So, it is evident that the plaintiff has no document, such as agreement, contract or bainapatra to prove her case.

22. The above factum led us to conclude that the plaintiff has been running after a fruitless litigation and in such a situation the law declared by our Appellate Division in the case of Abdul kW and others vs Islamic Bank Bangladesh Limited and others, (supra) is absolutely applicable in the facts and circumstances of the instant case. 

23. The above mentioned views were fortified in the case of Robi Axiata Ltd. vs First Labour Court, reported in 21 BLC (AD) 218, wherein the Appellate Division held:-- 
"...The Court can reject a plaint in exercise of inherent powers under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure if it is found that on the admitted facts that the plaint is otherwise barred by law. It further held that the Court should not feel helpless in circumstances to administer substantial justice and make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court. If the Court can exercise power for securing ends of justice, it can be said that the powers of the Court are wide enough and residuary in nature and not controlled by any other provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. It further held that in appropriate cases it can exercise its power to resolve a claim in order to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court or to fill up the lacuna left by legislature or where the legislature is unable to foresee any circumstances which may arise in a particular case." 

24. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant contends that the appellant has been staying and enjoying the possession of the suit flat since 2001 and has been paying all utility bills. However, in view of Annexure- 'E' series of the supplementary affidavit, we find the electricity bills, gas bills and service charges of co-operative society were paid in the name of one Mrs. Lipika Biswash (defendant No. 3). It is settled principle of law that mere permissive possession even for a long time does not confer title. 

25. The plaint shows that there is no document of title on the basis of the alleged gift which otherwise implies that the possession of the plaintiff in the suit flat is permissive in nature and the same never creates any title. Therefore, the instant suit is definitely barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. A court cannot grant declaration of title only on the basis of permissive possession and since the suit cannot run in accordance with law it should be buried at its inception. So, the trial Court has rightly rejected the plaint which is legally sound. 

26. It is evident that no agreement or contract exists between the plaintiff and defendants concerning the suit flat. Accordingly, the defendants have no obligation within the meaning of section 55 of the Specific Relief Act. Since no legal right or legal obligation has accrued in favour of the plaintiff, giving rise to a cause of action for mandatory injunction and the plaintiff has failed to establish her case for the grant of any injunction, she is not entitled to any decree in this regard. We find support in the decision rendered by the Appellate Division in the case of Aftab-uddin vs Mahfuzus Sobhan and others, (supra) wherein it was held:—
"Where the use of property is permissive and not as of right no case is made out for injunction far less a question of mandatory injunction. The obligation referred to in this section means a legal obligation and not a moral obligation." 27. In the light of foregoing discussion and observation, we find merit in the submissions made by Mr. Shafiullah regarding application of section 55 of the Specific Relief Act and find his contention to have substance. 

28. Given the above facts, circumstances of the case and discussion and observation made herein above, we are of the view that the learned Judge of the trial Court has rightly and legally rejected the plaint. 

29. Overall, we find no ground to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree. 

30. Resultantly, the appeal is dismissed, however without any order as to costs. 

31. The judgment and decree dated 21-8-2019 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 51 of 2019 is hereby affirmed.
 
32. The order of status-quo granted on 14-10-2019 by this Court stands recalled and vacated. 

Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the court concerned forthwith. 

End.

parties:
Fakhrul Islam being dead his heirs 1(a) Majeda Khatun and others ------ Petitioners
vs
Shamsul Huda Chowdhury being dead his heirs 1(a) Shafiqul Islam Chowdhury & others --------- Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Mozibur Rahman Miah, J: The predecessor of the decree holder in Other Class Execution Case No. 39 of 1986 namely, Shamsul Huda Chowdhury as plaintiff originally filed a suit being Other Class Suit No. 213 of 1966 in the court of the then Munsif, Cox's Bazar for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession in the suit land seeking following reliefs:— 
"(a) That the plaintiffs be given a decree for khas possession in the lands, houses etc, described in schedule "B" below by removing the unauthorized structure in schedule "c" below on the declaration of the plaintiffs title therein and against the defendants. 
(b) That the cost of the suit be decreed in favour of the plaintiff and against the contesting defendant. 
(c) That the defendant be directed to removed the unauthorized structure in schedule "C" at their own cost failing which the plaintiff be given the liberty to remove the same and to recover the cost thereof from the defendants. 
(d) That the plaintiff be given such other relief of reliefs as he may be found entitled in the circumstances of the case. 
(e) That the plaintiff be permitted to recover profits in a separate proceeding." 

2. That suit was contested by the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and the same was ultimately dismissed on contest against them on 16-7-1969 and thereby a decree was drawn up on 22-7-1969 by the then learned Munsif, Cox's Bazar. 

3. The plaintiff then preferred an appeal before the learned District Judge, Chittagong being Title Appeal No. 368 of 1969. The said appeal was on transfer heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd court, Chittagong and after hearing the parties, the said appeal was allowed and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif, Cox's Bazar was set-aside though it was sent back on remand to the trial court for fresh trial directing the learned Munsif to give a chance to the plaintiff to get the land of schedule 'B' relayed on commission and after getting the report decide the suit in accordance with law. 

4. After receiving the record on remand by the Munsif, the plaintiff was given chance for getting the suit land relayed on commission and thereby appointed a pleader commissioner for that purpose. Then the pleader commissioner upon giving notice to the parties to the suit, held local investigation and submitted his report on 2-9-1974 and the said report was accepted without any objection by the defendants. But ultimately the learned Munsif again dismissed the suit on 14-2-1978 and decree was drawn on 18-2-1978. 

5. Challenging the said judgment and decree of dismissal, the plaintiffs (decree holders) then preferred an appeal being other class appeal No. 138 of 1978 before the learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar which was on transfer heard by the learned Subordinate judge, Cox's Bazar who thus allowed the appeal on contest on 31-5-1982 and set-aside the judgment and decree passed by the learned Munsif, Cox's Bazar dated 14-2-1978 resulting in decreeing the suit. 

6. The defendants of the suit then preferred a Civil Revision being Civil Revision No. 32(c) of 1982 before the High Court Division against the said judgment and decree and a Circuit Bench of the High Court Division, Chittagong was pleased to upheld the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge by its judgment and order dated 22-6-1986 by discharging the rule. 

7. The defendants of the suit then preferred an appeal before the Appellate Di vision being Civil Petition for Leave to Special Appeal No. 211 of 1986. The Appellate Division also dismissed the said appeal on 25-9-1986 and upheld the judgment and order passed by this court in the Civil Revision dated 22-6-1986. After traveling up to the Appellate Division, the plaintiffs as a decree holders then initiated an Execution Case being Other Class Execution Case No. 39 of 1986. 

8. During the course of the execution case, the learned Munsit, Cox's Bazar on 15-12-1986 referred the matter before this court as of reference holding that—
"that this court being the execution court cannot go behind the decree. It can neither go for execution of the present decree which is admitted to be vague and unspecified on the one hand nor it can go for execution of the land as decide in the execution petition and in the writ of DP as per investigation report which is in fact not found in the decree the judgment debtor filed. That the learned advocate for the decree holder could not show any specific provision of laws or rules is/are to be followed in this regard when a question of law arises". 

9. Upon receiving the said reference, this court then registered it as Civil Reference No. 32 (C) of 1982 and it was accordingly placed before the then Hon'ble Chief Justice and he vide order dated 21-8-1989 placed the matter to a regular Division Bench to hear and dispose of the same when it was registered as Civil Reference No. 2 of 1991. During pendency of the said reference, for the last 34 years both the original decree holders as well as the judgment debtor died for which the heirs of the deceased were duly substituted. 

10. Mr. Abdul Momen Chowdhury, the learned senior counsel appearing for the decree holders at the very outset submits that, the reference referred by the then Munsif is totally misconceived and violative to Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and therefore the Civil Reference is liable to be rejected. 

11. The learned senior counsel further submits that, the learned Munsif has not stated a single word on what point this Hon'ble Court will give its opinion and decision and thereby the reference is untenable and the same is liable to be rejected. In addition to that, the learned counsel also submits that, since the decree was upheld by the apex court of this country and the defendants did not raise any objection with regard to the report submitted by the then pleader Commissioner on local investigation, so there has been no occasion to find schedule 'B' to the plaint is vague and unspecified that made him unable to execute the decree and therefore the assertion made in the reference by the learned Munsif cannot sustain in law. 

12. The learned counsel by referring to the provision of Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure then submits that, only a reference can be made before this Hon'ble court if any question of law or usage having the force of law arises but in the reference nothing sort of those are there which calls for any interference by this Hon'ble court and therefore the reference is liable to be rejected. However, in support of his submission the learned counsel has placed his reliance in the decision reported in 9 MLR (HC) 427. 

13. The learned counsel has also referred another two decisions of Indian jurisdiction reported in AIR 1968 Bombay 439(V55 C 74) as well as AIR 1970 Andhra Pradesh 365 and by quoting the ratio settled in that decision, the learned counsel then submits that, under the provision of section 113 and Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, it has been held in the said decision, "reference cannot be sought on hypothetical matter unless there is a pending case before the court which involves point of law determination of which is essential for the disposal of the case; so no question of reference can arise. Reference of hypothetical or imaginary questions or points likely to arise in cases that may be filed in future in view of the jurisdiction conferred on a court is wholly incompetent". 

14. Relying on the decisions, the learned counsel finally prays for rejecting the reference enabling the execution court to execute the decree which has been pending since 1986. 

15. Record shows, the judgment debtors did not represent the reference. 

16. We have considered the submission so placed by the learned senior counsel for the decree holders of Other Class Execution Case No. 39 of 1986 vis-à-vis the plaint in the Other Class Suit No. 213 of 1966 and perused the reference under challenge as well as the documents so have been annexed with the application for rejection of the reference filed by the decree-holders and the documents sent along with the reference by the court below. 

17. However, we feel it expedient to reproduce the provision provided in Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil procedure for our ready reference which runs as under:— 
"Order XLVI 
"(1) Where, before or on the hearing of a suit or an appeal in which the decree is not subject to appeal, or where, in the execution of any such decree, any question of law or usage having the force of law arises, on which the Court trying the suit or appeal, or executing the decree, entertains reasonable doubt, the Court may, either of its own motion or on the application of any of the parties, draw up a statement of the facts of the case and the point on which doubt is entertained, and refer such statement with its own opinion on the point for the decision of the High Court Division." 

18. On the face of the provision provided in Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, we find that, the lower court can only refer any matter to this court seeking reference if any question of law or usage having the force of law arises. Now, if we go through the finding of the learned the then Munsif, we find that he found that schedule "B" to the execution case is vague and unspecified for which he became unable to execute the decree. But he did not take into consideration of the judgment passed by the Appellate Division. It is on the record, on two consecutive occasions, the suit was dismissed by the then Munsif but the Munsif where the suit was sent back on remand however allowed the prayer of holding local investigation and the commissioner accordingly submitted his report which remained unchallenged by the defendants of the suit resulting in, the report has become valid in law and the same was tested even by the Appellate Division having no scope to raise any question with regard to vagueness of schedule 'B' property described in the plaint. On top of that, if we go through the provision laid down in Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure we clearly find that the reference can only be made by a lower court if any question of law or usage having the force of law arises but what the learned Munsif found compelling him to refer the matter is totally based on admitted fact as the defendants to the suit has not raised any objection against the investigation report filed by the advocate commissioner. So executing court can under no circumstances say the report is vague. So the learned Munsif had no other option but to execute the decree in terms of the report submitted by the advocate commissioner in respect of schedule '13' property as the decree passed in favour of the decree-holders was upheld by the Appellate Division. Be that as it may, we find ample substance to the submission so placed by the learned senior counsel for the decree-holders here in the objector because, the observation so made by the Munsif bears no legal substance. However, during hearing, we asked for the commissioner's report so submitted by the advocate commissioner when the learned senior counsel readily supplied photocopy of the same and on careful perusal, we find that the advocate commissioner preformed all the legal formalities while holding local investigation and filed report, Then again, on going through schedule '13' to the execution case, which has also been annexed by the decree holder in the written objection as of annexure 'g' we find that, there appears no ambiguity in executing decree especially, in regard to schedule '13' from where the plaintiff-decree holders alleged to have dispossessed by the defendants compelling him to sought recovery of khas possession and as the plaintiff-decree holders got the decree that was upheld up to the Appellate Division so the learned Munsif has got no other option but to execute the decree in line with the advocate commissioner's report. 

19. Regard being had to the above facts, circumstances and observation on legal point made herein above we don't find any iota of substance in the reference as it is not aligned with the provision of Order XLVI, rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure 

20. In the result, the reference is rejected however without any order as to costs. 

21. The learned Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar is hereby directed to execute the decree as expeditiously as possible preferably within a period of 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the copy of this order. 

Let a copy of this order along with the lower court records be communicated to the learned Assistant Judge, Cox's Bazar forthwith. 

End.

Abul Kalam Chowdhury with Iqbal Kalam Chowdhury, Shahin Miraz Chowdhury, Advocate—For the Petitioners.

parties:
Achia Katoon and others ------- Petitioners
vs
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Noakhali and others -------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
In this Civil Revision, the Rule was issued calling upon opposite party Nos.1-3 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 27-4-2010 (decree signed on 2-5-2010) passed by the 1st Court of learned Joint District Judge, Noakhali in Title Appeal No.202 of 2006 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 19-3-2006 (decree signed on 23-3-2006) passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Senbagh, Noakhali in Title Suit No.231 of 2003 decreeing the suit should not be set-aside and/or why such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper, shall not be passed. Pending the hearing of the Rule, the operation of the impugned appellate judgment and decree dated 27-4-2010 was stayed and the parties were directed to maintain a statusquo in respect of possession of the suit land initially for 6(six) months. Subsequently, the period of stay and status quo was extended from time to time. 

2. The petitioners as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.500 of 1979 in the 1st Court of Munsif, Sadar, Noakhali for declaration of title to the suit land described in the schedule to the plaint and also for a declaration that the proceeding of SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 which was initiated and concluded before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Noakhali is illegal and void. 

3. The plaintiffs' case, in short, is that defendant No.1 while was the owner of the lands described in the schedule to the plaint as property No.1 measuring 3.26 acres to plaintiff No.1 vide Settlement Case No.223 of 1954-1955 on receiving salami on 13-6-1958 and also receiving rent for it and accordingly, made delivery of possession. Following the said settlement, Khas Mohol Khatian No.1244 and holding No.1134 were opened in the name of plaintiff No.1. Accordingly; the land was also recorded in his name in SA Khatian No.471, and during the Diara survey, it was recorded in his name in Diara Khatian No.506. He has his homestead along with the dwelling house in the said property No.1. The land of property No.1 described in the schedule to the plaint measuring 2.50 acres was also settled by defendant No.1-Government to Hamid Ullah vide Settlement Case No.1068 of 1959-1960. On receiving salami and delivering possession of the same in his favour, Khas Mohol Khatian No.1271 and holding No.1162 were also opened in his name and accordingly, his name was also recorded in Diara Khatian No.545. Subsequently, Hamid Ullah sold the said land to Rafiqunnessa vide registered kabala dated 19-9-1968. Accordingly, Rafiqunnessa got her name mutated vide Mutation Case No.982 of 1973-1974. Then, she sold her land to plaintiff Nos.2-5 vide registered kabala dated 15-6-1977. Accordingly, plaintiff Nos.2-5 got their names mutated vide Mutation Case No.604 of 1978-1979, paid rent to the Government and they have been possessing their land by cultivation. The further case of the plaintiffs is that Abdul Awal got a settlement of 2.45 acres of land described as property No.3 in the schedule to the plaint. Accordingly, he paid salami, got possession and also paid rent. Subsequently, Abdul Awal sold his property to Abul Kashem, who subsequently sold the same to plaintiff No.6. Then, plaintiff No.6 sold 1.08 acres to one Abdul Awal, who purchased it in the benami of his son Abdur Rob, defendant No.4. Then, Abdul Awal sold his purchased land to plaintiff No.7 vide registered kabala dated 24-5-1976. The said land was recorded in the names of plaintiff Nos.6 and 7 in Diara Khatian No.255. Thus, plaintiff Nos.6 and 7 are owners of said property No.3. Plaintiff No.6 has his dwelling homestead in Diara Plot No.326 of the said land. Subsequently, plaintiff No.6 mortgaged the said land to Krishi Bank, Maijdee Court Branch and got a loan in 1978. Plaintiff No.7 also constructed a homestead on his portion. Thus, the plaintiffs are owners-in-possession of the land described in the schedule to the plaintiff. But the plaintiffs got a notice on 06-9- 1979 from defendant No.2 through the then-local Circle Officer regarding some of the lands of the plaintiffs. In the said notice, it was alleged that SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 was started against the plaintiffs for recovery of the same as the land of the police department .:rider the provision of Ordinance No.XXII of 1970. The plaintiffs filed an objection thereto stating their claim on the land, but the plaintiffs' lawyer was not allowed to peruse the records of the said case. Subsequently, two local police constables threatened the plaintiffs on 15-9-1979 to vacate the said land to the police department otherwise, they would be sent to jail while the defendants have no right, title or possession in the suit land. The plaintiffs are owners-in-possession of the suit land. Accordingly, the plaintiffs filed the instant suit. 

4. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the suit by filing a written statement. It was stated in the written statement that the suit land was acquired for the police department and educational department. The suit land is khas land of the Government. The suit land was acquired vide LA Case No.4 of 1908-1909 and accordingly, it was duly recorded in the name of the school in DS Khatian No.1186. The suit land was diluviated and alluviated land. The suit land was never settled for the plaintiffs. Khatian No.506 in the name of the plaintiff is false, Lands of DS Khatian No.1177/1 were acquired for the police department vide LA Miscellaneous Case No.2 of 1971-1972. Khatian No.545 in the name of the plaintiffs is also false. Lands of DS Khatian No.1177/1 was also acquired for the jail department vide LA Miscellaneous Case No.3 of 1981. Thus, the Diara Khatian in the names of the plaintiffs is fraudulent. SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 was started for the suit land. Accordingly, the plaintiffs have no right, title or possession in the suit land and hence, the suit is liable to be dismissed. 

5. Defendant No.3, Superintendent of Police, Noakhali also contested the suit by filing a separate written statement. It was the case of defendant No.3 that during the British Era, the suit land was owned by the Government, and it was within the then Noakhali Pourasava and former Noakhali District Headquarters. The Government allotted it to the police department for the accommodation of police officers, parade grounds and fire service station and accordingly, the police department used it for the same purposes. Later, it was diluviated and alluviated within 20 years. The said land was also recorded in the name of the police department in DS Khatian Nos.9/2, 9/5, 1177/1 and 1183. The plaintiffs created papers for grabbing the land in collusion with the officials and obtained an illegal order of lease. The settlement claimed by the plaintiffs was not acted upon. The police department was the owner of the suit land. Accordingly, the suit is liable to be dismissed. Defendant No.3 also filed an additional written statement wherein the title of the Government in the suit land was also denied. 

6. During the trial, the plaintiffs called for the records of the necessary documents relating to the lease of the suit land. Subsequently, the suit was transferred to the Court of Learned Assistant Judge, Senbagh, Noakhali and it was renumbered as Title Suit No.221 of 2003. 

7. During the trial, the plaintiffs examined 4(four) witnesses while defendant Nos.1 and 2 examined only 1(one) witness but, defendant No.3 did not adduce and produce either any documentary or oral evidence. The plaintiffs' documents were marked as Exhibits 1-13 while defendant Nos.1 and 2 did not produce any documentary evidence. 

8. After hearing both the parties, the learned Trial Court by the judgment and decree dated 19-3-2006 (decree signed on 23-3-2006) decreed the suit. 

9. Against the judgment and decree of the Trial Court, defendant Nos.1-3 preferred Title Appeal No.202 of 2006 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Noakhali. The appeal was transferred to the 1st Court of Learned Joint District Judge, Noakhali for its disposal. During the hewing of the appeal, the appellant filed some documents which were marked as Exhibits-Ka series. The Appellate Court, after hearing both the parties, by the judgment and decree dated 27-4-2010 (decree signed on 2-5-2010) allowed the appeal, set-aside and reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court. 

10. Against the judgment and decree of the Appellate Court, the plaintiffs as petitioners filed the instant Civil Revision and obtained the Rule and the interim order of stay and status quo. 

11. Having placed the Civil Revision, Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury along with Mr Iqbal Kalam Chowdhury and Mr Shahin Miraz Choudhury, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the Court of Appeal below failed to consider that following the proceeding of SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980, the DS Khatians, Exhibit-Ka series was prepared but, the initiation and conclusion of the said SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 have no basis as regarding such claim that the land belonged to the police department was not proved by producing any document while even, said DS Khatian was not legally and formally proved and marked as Exhibits by the Court of Appeal below and, as such„ the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below is liable to be declared to have been passed illegally and upon misreading the material evidence on records and thereby, the Court of Appeal below committed errors of law resulting in errors in the decree occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that apart from the certified copies of four DS Khatians, defendant Nos.1-3 could not produce any other document in support of the claim of the defendants. On the other hand, the plaintiffs produced all the relevant documents regarding the Settlement Cases and rent receipts and subsequent documents of title and accordingly, the Trial Court having meticulously perused and examined the material evidence on records rightly decreed the suit and on the contrary, the Court of Appeal below without reversing those material findings and observations of the Trial Court mechanically reversed and set-aside the judgment and decree of the Trial Court and thus, the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below being not a proper judgment and decree of reversal, the same is liable to be set-aside as thereby, the Court of Appeal below committed errors of law resulting in errors in the decree occasioning failure of justice. The Trial Court having considered the depositions of the PWs rightly came to the decision that the plaintiffs are in possession of the suit land either by constructing a dwelling house or by cultivation. On the other hand, the defendant-appellant could not prove their title and possession in the suit land but, the Court of Appeal below merely on surmise, conjecture and inference on four DS Khatians came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs have no right, title and possession in the suit land and thus, the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below suffer from non-application of judicial mind and misreading of material evidence on record and thereby, the Court of Appeal below committed errors of law resulting in errors in the decree occasioning failure of justice and hence, the Rule should be made absolute and the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below should be set-aside. 

12. On the other hand, Mr Md Shafiquel Islam Siddique, learned Deputy Attorney-General along with Mr Sajid Ahamed Choudhury, learned Assistant Attorney-General and Mr Mohammad Nurul Amin, learned Assistant Attorney-General having appeared on behalf of the defendant-appellant-opposite parties submits that the Diara Khatian is the prima fade evidence of possession of the defendant-appellant-opposite parties in the suit land and, as such„ the Court of Appeal below rightly held that the so-called settlements in the names of the plaintiffs or their predecessor in interest were not acted upon and thus, there being no legal infirmity in the judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below, the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

13. I have perused the Civil Revision along with the records of the Courts below and heard the learned Advocate for the petitioners and the learned Deputy Attorney-General for the opposite parties. 

14. There is no dispute that the suit land originally belonged to the Government. But as per the plaintiffs' case, they got the suit land vide three Settlement Cases, Settlement Case Nos.223 of 1954-1955, 1068 of 1959-1960 and 892 of 1959-1960. Accordingly, following the said three Settlement Cases, Khas Mohol Khatian Nos.1244, 1271 and 5822 were opened and accordingly, they paid salami and rent and similarly, a separate holding of the land was also opened in the name of the said settlement receivers. The plaintiffs are claiming the suit land either by way of inheritance or by purchase from the settlement receivers and after such settlement or purchase, they have been possessing the respective lands by constructing homesteads, including the dwellinghouse or by cultivation. 

15. On the other hand, the case of the defendants is that the suit land was acquired by the Government vide LA Case No.4 of 1908-1909 and it was recorded in the name of a school in DS Khatian No.1186. It was also the admitted case of both the parties that the suit land was diluviated and alluviated. Subsequently, the lands appertaining to DS Khatian No.1177/1 were acquired for the police department vide LA Miscellaneous Case No.2 of 1971-1972 and also vide LA Miscellaneous Case No.3 of 1981 in favour of the jail authority. However, the defendants could not produce any document in support of such LA Cases. 

16. It appears from the records of the Trial Court that the defendants took adjournment of the suit on several occasions for producing the documents relating to the said LA Cases. Even DW1 in his deposition said that he would not and could not produce any document in support of such LA Cases. Subsequently, in the Appellate Court, the defendant-appellant also could not produce any document regarding such LA Cases. 

17. During the hearing of the instant Civil Revision, by order dated 2-3-2023, the Government-opposite parties were also allowed to produce the documents if any, relating to the said LA Cases but today, at the time of the pronouncement of judgment, the learned Deputy Attorney-General produced a Memo dated 12-3-2023 issued by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Noakhali. From the said Memo, it appears that no document is available regarding the said LA Cases. Let the said Memo dated 12-3-2023 be kept with the record. 

18. It also appears from the case of the defendants that they did not even cancel the said three settlement cases. Accordingly, the said three settlement cases are still in force. In such facts and circumstances, the Trial Court found that the Government could not prove any right, title, interest and possession in the suit land but, defendant No.2, Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Noakhali issued a notice dated 6-9-1979 through the then local Circle Officer stating that SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 was started against the plaintiffs for recovery of the land for the police department under the provision of Ordinance No.XXII of 1970 and then, the police department threatened the plaintiffs to vacate the suit land in favour of the defendants. But it does not appear from the defendants' case that the Government acquired the property in favour of the police department vide LA Miscellaneous Case No.2 of 1971-1972. It has already been found that the defendants could not produce any document in support of such an Case. Therefore, the initiation of the proceeding of the said SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 had no basis. Thus, the defendants completely failed to prove that the Government or the police department has any right, title, interest or possession in the suit land. But it appears from the records of the Court of Appeal below that during the hearing of the appeal on 23-3-2010, the defendant-appellant filed an application for admission as evidence of the certified copies of DS Khatian Nos.9/5, 1183, 1177/1 and 9/2 which were produced from the office of the Superintendent of Police, Noakhali. 

19. It further appears from the order dated 23-3-2010 passed by the Court of Appeal below that even without examining any witness, the said DS Khatians were marked as Exhibits-Ka(1), Ka(2) and Ka(3). Therefore, the said certified copies of the alleged DS Khatians were not at all formally proved; rather, upon admission of such documents as evidence without providing any chance of the plaintiff-respondents to controvert those documents by cross-examining any defendant witnesses and thereby, the Court of Appeal below further committed an error of law in admitting such document as evidence even without examining any witness. Moreover, it has already been found that such DS Khatians have no basis, while the settlement in favour of the plaintiffs or their predecessor in interest still exists and is in force. So long as the said settlement exists, the Government cannot claim any title or take over possession of the land covered by the said settlement cases. 

20. Accordingly, the Trial Court rightly declared the proceeding of the said SA Miscellaneous Case No.39 of 1979-1980 as illegal and void. Since the Government cannot claim possession of any land that has already been settled in favour of a citizen nor is any department of the Government legally authorized to take over possession of any land of any citizen forcibly or illegally and, as such, I do not find any legal infirmity in the judgment and decree of the Trial Court. But the Court of Appeal below without considering the material evidence on the record as well as the relevant provision of law reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court merely on surmise, conjecture and inference on the said four DS Khatians purportedly prepared in the name of the police department while, it has already been found that there is no basis of such DS Khatians. 

21. Accordingly, the Court of Appeal below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decree occasioning failure of justice by passing such perfunctory judgment and decree without considering the material evidence on record and hence, I find merit in the Rule. 

22. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. 

23. The judgment and decree of the Court of Appeal below is hereby set-aside and the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court is upheld. 

24. The interim order of stay and status quo granted earlier by this Court is hereby recalled and vacated. 

25. However, there would be no order as to costs. 

Send down the records of the Courts below immediately. 

End.
