case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 5th May, 1966 passed by the Dacca High Court in S.A.No.918 of 1963.)
full_judgment:
Ahsanuddin Chowdhury, J. —This appeal by special leave, at the instance of the plaintiffs is from the judgment passed in Second Appeal No. 918 of 1963 by the erstwhile High Court of East Pakistan.

2. The plaintiffs filed a suit being Title Suit No. 327 of 1961 in the 1st Court of Munsif at Perojpur for establishment of their title to 4 annas share in the suit land and for confirmation of their possession therein. They also made an alternative prayer for recovery of possession of that land, if they were found to be out of possession. Their case was that the land of C.S. Plot No. 929 appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 149 of mouza Kalakhali under P.S. Perojpur, District Barisal belonged to Ekramullah to the extent of 8 annas, Islam Sikdar and Kalim Sikdar to the extent of 4 annas each in Karasha right. The 4 annas share of Islam Sikdar devolved upon the plaintiffs and that of Kalim Sikdar was inherited by his daughters defendant Nos. 18 and 19. Ekramullah granted a Patta in 1305 B.S. in Kol Karsha right in respect of his 8 annas share to Alimuddin and Tasiluddin, predecessors-in-interest of defendant Nos.1 to 12. In Augrahayan, 1368 B.S. corresponding to December, 1961 the defendants threatened the plaintiffs with dispossession whereupon the aforesaid suit was filed.

3. Defendant No. 4 contested the suit. His case was that Ekramullah was in exclusive possession of the entire land of plot No. 929 and on 10th Falgoon, 1305 B.S. he granted a Patta to Tasiluddin and Alimuddin who possessed the property and now defendants 1-12 have been exclusively possessing the entire land claiming their sixteen annas interest therein openly to the knowledge of the plaintiffs. Accordingly he denied plaintiffs title and possession therein.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit, found plaintiffs title to the suit land and awarded them joint possession therein with the defendants. On appeal by the defendant, the judgment and decree of the trial Court were set aside and the suit was dismissed as being barred by time on the finding that the defendants have been possessing the suit land adversely to the plaintiffs openly to the knowledge of the latter for more than 12 years from the date of institution of the suit. Plaintiffs appealed to the High Court against the judgment and decree of the first appellate Court without any success. Thereafter they obtained the special leave to appeal.

Leave was granted to consider as to whether the possession of the defendant-respondents who are lessees under a co-sharer of the plaintiff-appellants will be adverse to the latter and will amount to ouster.

5. Mr. S.R. Pal, learned Counsel for the appellants contended that the defendant-respondents claim their title and possession in the suit land on the basis of their settlement from Ekramullah who is admittedly one of the co-sharers in the holding to which the suit land appertains. Their case, however, is that Ekramullah while in exclusive possession of the entire land settled the same with them and since then they have exclusively possessed the entire land. It was accordingly claimed that the right, title and interest of the appellants, if any, had long been barred by time, learned counsel referred us in this connection to the findings of the courts below with a view to show how the question was approached by them. The trial Court found:-

“It is not disputed that property in C.S. Khatian No. 149 is still ejmali. Hence all the co-sharers have shares and possession in all the land of the Khatian. The C.S. Khatian No. 149 shows that the dag No.929 was recorded in the sole possession of Ekram. There is no specific case of ouster or adverse possession by Ekram in the dag. There is no convincing evidence on record in this respect. Hence, all the co-sharers have their shares in this dag as well as in all the plots of C.S. Khatian No. 149.”

“The documents filed by the parties give rise to a strong presumption that defdts. 1-12 possessed the land, that plffs. and defdts. 18-19 had no actual possession in the suit land. Be it as it may all the co-sharers have constructive possession in every plot of the properly along with other co-sharers.

The first appellate Court came to the following findings:-

The oral evidence adduced by the defendants coupled with the documentary evidence in their favor led me to believe that the defendants are in possession of the entire suit land. So from the above discussion I am inclined to hold that the plaintiffs are kept out of possession by the defendants for more than 12 years.”

* * * *

“Since the plaintiffs have been ousted for more than 12 years by the defendants to their knowledge they cannot have any relief whatsoever in this suit”.

The High Court arrived at the following findings in the Second Appeal:-

“It seems that adverse possession openly and to the knowledge of the plaintiffs has been inferred by the appellate Court below from the documentary as well as oral evidence.”

<u>6. Mr. Pal urged that although it was found that Ekramullah alone possessed C.S. plot No. 929 and now the lessees under him have been possessing the same, the first appellate Court as well as the High Court erred in holding that the said possession amounted to adverse possession to the knowledge of the appellants and that it constituted ouster. He argued that it is neither unusual nor inconceivable that a co-sharer may keep in his sole possession certain plot of a joint holding. This possession simply amounted to sole possession of a co-sharer and such sole possession does not amount to exclusive or adverse possession constituting ouster. He pointed out that Khatian No. 149 contains several plots including the suit pot No. 929 and it is not disputed that the land of this Khatian is still joint among the co-sharers. He further pointed out that joint possession of all the co-sharers was recorded in Khatian No. 149 according to their shares vide Ext. D. But the kolkarsha of the respondents in plot No. 929 was recorded under Ekramullah. Nevertheless the legal title that is Karsha right of the other co-sharers in respect of this plot was not affected. The respondents cannot claim more than Kolkarsha right which they took settlement of from Ekramullah. They did not ever deny the superior karsha right of Ekramullah. The appellants claim their karsha right along with their co-sharer Ekramullah. In this view of the matter it was urged that the Courts of appeal below erred in dismissing the suit on the finding that the title of co-sharers had been lost due to adverse possession of the respondents. In support of his contention he relied upon some decisions. In Bindu Bala De Vs. Rebati Mohan De (4 DLR Dac. 239) the question arose about the effect of a record standing in the name of one of the co-sharers of a joint property. It was contended that the properly was in exclusive possession of the person in whose favor the record stood. It was, however, held "if a joint property is recorded in the possession of one of the co-sharers, the effect of the record is that it was in the sole possession of that co-sharers and it would not raise an inference that it was in his exclusive possession or in his possession adversely to the other co-sharers as sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession" It is in conformity with the well settled principle of law that possession of one co-sharer is in point of law the possession of all co-sharers. In Arjun Chandra Vs. Jogendra Chandra (13 DLR Dac. 565) there was a question as to whether the transferee from a co-tenant was on the same footing as original tenant in the matter of the rules governing relations between tenants in common. It was observed that transferee from a co-tenant was on the same footing as the original tenant in the matter of the rules governing relations between tenants-in-common. The rule that possession of a co-sharer is presumed to be non-adverse against the other co-sharers is applied to the transferees as well. The possession by a co-owner of a joint property is perfectly lawful as he is not only entitled to his undivided share but to the whole of the property. There is, therefore, no bar for an owner of an undivided share to the property to be in possession of the whole of that property, but his possession on basis of legal right cannot be adverse to the other co-sharers. The learned counsel thus submitted that the same principle must govern the case of lessees from a co-sharer of a joint property so far as their possession is concerned. Reliance was placed on a decision reported in  A.I.R. 1936 P.C. 183 (Pannambala Vs. Periyanan) with a view to show that possession of lessees does not become adverse till something is done repudiating tenancy. He, therefore, rightly urged that the possession of the respondents in the suit land being under a co-sharer of the appellants, however long and continuous this possession may be, it cannot be adverse so long hostile title is not set up by the lessees against their own lessor and that is possible only after repudiation of the tenancy. It may be noted that the respondents did not ever deny the title of their lessor Ekramullah.</u>

<u>7. Learned counsel next argued that uninterrupted possession of a co-sharer or lessees under him for any length of time will be of no avail unless the said possession is exercised with assertion of hostile and independent title through adverse possession denying openly and notoriously the title of the co-sharers. That is to say, ouster is necessary to constitute adverse possession by a co-sharer. Mere sole possession of a joint estate by any one of the co-sharers affords no evidence to exclusion of the co-sharers having interest. There is also authority in support of the proposition that uninterrupted possession of a property must be referred to the lawful title possessed by the co-sharer of the joint estate and cannot be regarded as an assertion of a right to hold it as separate so as to assert an adverse claim against other co-sharers having interest therein. When the question arises, as to whether the possession is either lawful or unlawful it must be assumed in the absence of evidence to the contrary, that the possession is lawful not only on his behalf but on behalf of his co-owners. In support of this proposition reference may be made to two decisions of the Privy Council, C.R.V. S. Corea Vs. M.I. Appuhamy (A.I.R. 1914 P.C. 243) and W.P. Tamel Vs. H.A. Anohamy (A.I.R. 1918 P.C. 339). Learned counsel in conclusion submitted that the trial Court rightly decreed the suit and that the first appellate Court as well as the High Court committed errors in law in finding that the respondent's possession was adverse to the appellants who are co-sharers of respondents lessor and in holding that the said possession constituted their ouster from the property.</u>

8. Mr. T. Ali, learned counsel for the respondents argued that though Ekramullah had 8 annas share in the property, he granted the para Ext. A of the entire plot to Tasiluddin and Alimuddin in 1305 B.S. Since then this entire plot was possessed by them and now by defendants 1-12 who are respondents, to the knowledge of the appellants who never raised any objection to the possession of the respondents. In view of the point of law involved in this case, the question whether Ekramullah granted lease in respect of his 8 annas share or entire plot is immaterial because it as been found that Ekramullah was in sole possession of the entire plot as a co-sharer.

9. Mr. Ali sought to argue that respondents long and uninterrupted possession for more than 30 years must be held to have constituted ouster by adverse possession. He relied upon some cases in support of his contention, namely, Ayenenussa Bibi Vs. Sheikh Isuf (16 C.W.N. 849), Chaitanya Krishna Mandal Vs. Sandhy Amani Dasi (27 C.W.N. 624), The Secy. of State for India in Council Vs. Debendra Lal Khan (38 C.W.N. PC 285) and Gangadhar Vs. Parashram (I.L.R. 29 Bom. 300).

<u>10. We feel no hesitation to say that the principle enunciated in those cases have no conflict with what we have said above. In Ayenunussa Bibi Vs. Sheikh Isuf (16 C.W.N. 349) it has been observed that to establish adverse possession by one tenant-in-common against his co-tenants there must be exclusion or ouster and the possession subsequent to that must be for the statutory period. Mere non-participation to rents and profits would not necessarily of itself amount to exclusion. Similar view has been expressed in the other cases too. It is settled law that to constitute ouster by adverse possession, the possession must not only be open, notorious and continuous, it must also be in assertion of hostile title against the party claiming their title to the property. In the instant case it has no doubt been found by all the Courts below that defendants 1-12 have been possessing the land continuously for a long period. But the question is whether this long and uninterrupted possession will amount to adverse possession constituting ouster of admitted co-sharers of the lessor of the defendants who have not at any point of time denied the title of their lessor who is a co-sharer of the plaintiffs-appellants. The clear finding of the trial Court is that there is no case of ouster by adverse possession and that no evidence was also adduced to that effect. Mere sole possession for a long time is not enough to put an end to the legal title of a co-sharer. It has already been observed that the sole possession is not exclusive or adverse possession unless it is openly and notoriously claimed that the said possession is in assertion of hostile or independent title. This claim is in the eye of law lacking in this case inasmuch as without repudiating the tenancy under Ekramullah such a claim is not sustainable.</u>

11. The possession of the respondents being under a co-sharer of the appellants cannot be held to be adverse to the appellants claiming their superior right, namely, Rarsha right with that of the respondents lessor. Plaintiff-appellants title to the land is not therefore barred by time. Learned Munsif rightly found that the plaintiffs (appellants) have got their title to the extent of 4 annas share in karsha right and they are, in the eye of law, in constructive possession as co-sharers therein and they have been rightly awarded joint possession with their co-sharers in superior right, namely, karsha right. The Courts of appeal below did not correctly approach the question of title and possession claimed by the plaintiffs (appellants) in the suit land.

In the result, the appeal succeeds and it is allowed. The judgment of the erstwhile High Court and of the first appellate Court are set aside and that of the Munsif is restored without, however, any order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
Mr. Muhammad unman Ali, J :- This civil petition for leave to appeal is filed against the judgment and order dated 28.05.2012 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.5870 of 2007 discharging the Rule.

2. The petitioner and the proforma respondents before us, filed the aforementioned .suit, seeking cancellation of (1) a wasiyatnama dated 30.05.1970 (2) a cancellation deed (3) a Helm deed dated 05.01.71 and (4) a sale kabala dated 05.11.1971.

3. The averments of the plaintiffs as appearing in their pleading is, in gist, to the effect that the executant of all these documents named Kazi Abdul Mazid.is the father of the plaintiffs and of defendant No.1 and that their said father, who died on 9.2.71 was fully disabled physically and mentally form 1968 till his last breath, and that defendant No.1 in whose house their disabled father lived during his last days, fraudulently, with the connivance of some functionaries at the sub-Registry office, obtained their said father's LTI, to manufacture all these deeds pretending transfer of late Majid's properties the to the said defendant.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit by declaring that the deeds in question are illegal, fraudulent, null and void and not binding upon the plaintiffs.

5. The appellate Court, however, allowed the appeal and thereby reversed the trial Court's judgment and decree, stating that the trial Court failed to analyse the evidence prudently.

6. The High Court Division, then, in disposing of the civil revisional application filed by the plaintiff discharged the Rule. The plaintiff is now before us, having filed the instant civil petition for leave to appeal.

7. The High Court Division observed that the suit was not maintainable in view of Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act as (i) no consequential relief was sought. (ii) a registered deed carries a rebuttable presumption of authenticity, (iii) the plaintiff failed to prove that his father, the executant, was physically and mentally incapacitated to execute the deeds.

8. To press the leave petition, Mr. Abdul Haque the learned Advocate for the leave petitioner argued that the High Court Division misread the transcript of evidence and also the admitted facts and the materials on record. He went on to submit that the onus of proving genuineness of the documents lay on the defendants.

9. After going through the judgments of the Courts below upon perusing the transcript of evidence, and analyzing the relevant laws we remain firmly convinced as to the total accuracy of the High court Division's judgment and Order.

10. It is definitely not a case for mere declaration, because by a mere declaration the whole episode could not be brought to a final end, as without canceling the impugned deeds the dispute between the parties would have remained unresolved and hence, seeking consequential relief in the form of orders for the cancellations of deeds, were absolutely imperative.

11. The High Court Division was also quite as true in holding that the plaintiff failed to prove the executant's incapacitated mental and physical health. While it is true that the plaintiff by his oral testimony spoke of the executant's said state of health at the relevant time, evidence in the form of medical certificate is really desired to substantiate such a claim as only an expert witness can accurately depose on such a phenomenon.

12. In this respect we find the leave petitioner's contention on onus, quite erroneous and ill conceived. The rule of evidence as is universally acclaimed and recognized in common law areas, is that one who asserts must prove. This follows that since it is the plaintiffs who asserted that the documents were obtained by deceitful devices, the onus is fully on them to establish that said assertion by adducing evidence. The burden would shift to the defendants, if and only if, the plaintiffs could discharge their initial burden of proving what they claimed, the standard of proving, however, being balance of probability which is the civil standard.

13. We are in full accord with the High Court Division so far as its observation on the rebuttable presumption of genuineness is concerned. The language in section 60 of the Registration Act is clear enough to dean that a registered document carries a strong presumption to the effect that the procedure was properly followed. Indeed that is what the Privy Council observed in the case of Purshotom Das (33 IA 60).

<u>14. In similar vein, this Division in Abani Mohan vs. Asst. Custodian (SDO) of the Vested Property, Chandpur and others, 39 DLR (AD) 223, observed that if the question is whether the deed is genuine or not, the simple answer is, it being a registered document, is showered with a strong presumption as to genuineness Sections 59. 79 and 114 of the Evidence Act also lend support to Section 60 of the Registration Act on this score. No doubt, this presumption is rebuttable, which connotes that presumption raised by the admitted fact of registration could he rebutted by adducing countervailing evidence, showing that notwithstanding the fact of registration, the executant did not really affix his signature or thumb impression voluntarily which in the given circumstances, could be done by adducing expert evidence as to the physical and/or mental incapacity of the executant.</u>

15. In view of the above, we not find any merit in the instant civil petition for leave to appeal, which is accordingly dismissed.

End.
